column4: The section's wording is “yukadhdhibu bi'l-din”; 82:9 says “تُكَذِّبُونَ بِالدِّينِ” of the deniers, an almost exact formulation that names the act at the center of 107:1.
The section's dictionary form explains dīn as judgment, accounting, and recompense; al-Fātiḥa names Allah as “مَٰلِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” locating the account with its owner.
The section pictures an account ledger whose lines come due; here the book leaves nothing small or great unrecorded, and the wrongdoers fear what it contains.
The section's debt ledger makes acts answerable; this ayah says each person's record is fastened to them and brought out on Resurrection Day.
The section imagines the account being settled; “اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ” tells the person to read their own book, which suffices as reckoner.
The section's dictionary form داينت names giving or taking a debt; “إِذَا تَدَايَنتُم بِدَيْنٍ ... فَاكْتُبُوهُ” gives the literal written debt ledger behind that image.
The section names withholding as the opposite of giving; this ayah says that when good touches a person, “مَنُوعًا” describes them as withholding, the same refusal made concrete.
The section says the poor person's share is not mentioned; here the faithful have “حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ” in their wealth, a specified right rather than a discretionary favor.
The section says the poor person's share is omitted; this ayah assigns the known right to “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ,” the asker and deprived person.
The section connects denying dīn with denying the settled account; this ayah describes the faithful as those who “يُصَدِّقُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” affirming that day.
The section says the needy person's portion is a right; this ayah puts “حَقٌّ” in believers' wealth for “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ,” the asker and deprived.
The section describes the miskīn's right as left unmentioned; this command says to give the miskīn and traveler their due, making the neglected share explicit.
The section links refusal of the final account to withholding what is due; this ayah joins “لَا يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ” with being disbelievers in the Hereafter.
The section quotes this divine question to the human who lives as if no account awaits: “مَا غَرَّكَ بِرَبِّكَ الْكَرِيمِ” asks what has deluded them about their generous Lord.
The section's central phrase is denial of dīn; this ayah explicitly calls the condemned “الَّذِينَ يُكَذِّبُونَ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ.”
The section's dictionary account culminates in a day people can deny; the speakers here confess “نُكَذِّبُ بِيَوْمِ الدِّينِ,” directly naming that denial.
The section says the poor person's food is not urged; among the condemned speakers here, “لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ” names failure to feed the poor as part of their account.
The section says the denier does not even urge food for the poor; this ayah uses the same formulation, “وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ,” as the reason in the condemned person's portrait.
The section pictures the orphan being thrust aside; this rebuke says “لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ,” failing to honor the orphan, exposing the social neglect behind the image.
The section says no one urges the poor person's food; this ayah likewise reproaches people for not urging one another to feed the miskīn.
The section's orphan is pushed away; this command, “فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ,” sets the direct boundary against overpowering or oppressing an orphan.
The section depicts inattentive prayer; in the answer about why they entered Saqar, these speakers say “لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ الْمُصَلِّينَ,” placing prayer among the neglected duties.
The section's full surah exposes prayer performed carelessly and for display; this ayah describes hypocrites rising lazily for prayer and “يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ,” showing people.
The section's dictionary form glosses dīn as obedience and its ending glosses al-māʿūn as obedience and zakāh; this ayah joins sincere worship, prayer, and zakāh as the commanded dīn.
The section sets the surah's negligent worshippers against the exception in al-Maʿārij; this ayah begins that exception: “إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ.”
The section cites the prayerful exception to 107's distracted worshippers; this ayah specifies that they “دَائِمُونَ,” steadfastly maintain their prayer.
The section gathers the surah's refusal and neglect into a human portrait; this passage opens by calling humankind “هَلُوعًا,” then describes the behavior that the faithful exception reverses.

This continues the human portrait begun at 70:19 and completed by 70:21, describing the impatient response when evil touches a person; it supplies the other side of the unstable character whose response to good is withholding.
This continues the faithful portrait after 70:26's affirmation of the Day of Dīn: they are “مُشْفِقُونَ” of their Lord's punishment, showing how belief in the account shapes conduct.
This completes the fear introduced at 70:27: no one is secure from the Lord's punishment. It gives the weight behind the section's account and recompense image.
Continuing the same portrait after 70:26, this ayah says the faithful keep their trusts and covenants; it makes the section's debt and due-paying image an ethical obligation.
This continues the faithful portrait after its prayer, wealth-right, and dīn details at 70:22–26, specifying that they guard their prayers—the reverse of 107's heedlessness.

The section records the dictionary idiom كذب عليكم الحج as meaning that Hajj is incumbent; this ayah states the duty as “وَلِلَّهِ عَلَى النَّاسِ حِجُّ الْبَيْتِ,” pilgrimage to the House being due from people.

This completes the debt-writing passage at 2:282: when a debtor is trusted, the one entrusted must “فَلْيُؤَدِّ الَّذِي اؤْتُمِنَ أَمَانَتَهُ,” fulfill the trust, making repayment a matter of fidelity.

The section develops literal borrowing and repayment as an image for divine recompense; this ayah asks who will lend Allah a good loan for multiplication, turning the debt relation toward generous giving.
The section's debt dictionary branch meets the Qur'anic image of lending to God: “قَرْضًا حَسَنًا” is multiplied for the lender, giving generosity a promised return.
This repeats the good-loan image connected to the section's debt-and-recompense relation: a loan to Allah is multiplied and forgiven.
This ayah joins the section's motifs in one context: establish prayer, give zakāh, and offer Allah “قَرْضًا حَسَنًا,” so worship and material due are both forms of obedience.
The section's al-māʿūn dictionary form includes giving and zakāh; this ayah promises generous reward to men and women who give charity and lend Allah a good loan.

The section's orphan and poor are people whose share is refused; this account of righteousness includes giving wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, so righteousness is measured by what reaches them.
The section treats the poor's portion as a due; this ayah assigns zakāh to the poor and needy among named recipients, making distribution a defined obligation.
The section names the poor person's missing food; this ayah describes feeding on a day of hunger as a steep moral passage.
The section's orphan is denied care; this ayah specifies feeding “يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ,” an orphan of kin, as part of that passage.
The section's neglected miskīn is made visible here as “مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ,” a poor person in dust, completing the feeding scene begun in 90:14.
The section's orphan is denied the care due to them; this ayah names the more specific abuse of consuming orphans' property unjustly and its punishment, showing the account attached to their rights.
This continues the giving-and-rights passage at 17:26: it forbids approaching an orphan's property except in the best way, extending the section's due-paying image to guardianship of the vulnerable.
The section's whole surah condemns giving only to be seen; this ayah describes people who spend wealth to show off before others, connecting display to the use of wealth.
The section's prayer-and-charity portrait includes “يُرَاءُونَ”; this ayah warns that spending for show, “رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ,” can void charity, exposing the opposite of giving as a true due.
The section names withholding as the opposite of giving; this ayah condemns those who are “يَبْخَلُونَ” with what Allah gave them from His bounty, and says it will be placed around their necks.
The section's refused due is reversed by the person who gives and is mindful; this ayah joins giving (أَعْطَىٰ) to fear of God and affirmation of the best reward.
This continues the giving portrait begun at 92:5: the person “صَدَّقَ بِالْحُسْنَىٰ” affirms the good, a counter-image to the section's denier of dīn.
The giving and affirmation of 92:5–6 receive ease toward ease; this gives the section's account image a positive outcome for the one who answers rightly.
Against the section's al-māʿūn as benefit and gift, this ayah describes one who is stingy and thinks himself self-sufficient, the posture behind withholding.
This completes the reverse portrait begun at 92:8: the person denies the best reward, matching the section's denial of the account while refusing what is due.
This completes the fate in 92:8–9: the withholding denier is eased toward hardship, a contrary outcome to the ease granted to the giver in 92:7.
The section's dīn dictionary form means judgment and recompense; Abraham hopes that God will forgive his sin “يَوْمَ الدِّينِ,” locating forgiveness within that accounting day.
The section's Day of Dīn is the day the account is faced; the condemned exclaim “هَٰذَا يَوْمُ الدِّينِ” when they are raised.
This completes 37:20 by identifying the day as “هَٰذَا يَوْمُ الْفَصْلِ,” the judgment the deniers had called false, clarifying what the section's account brings.
The section treats dīn as the certain day of reckoning; this ayah says “إِنَّ الدِّينَ لَوَاقِعٌ,” that the judgment/recompense is surely coming.
The section's dictionary form glosses the Day of Dīn as recompense; this ayah calls the punishment of the people of the left their provision on “يَوْمِ الدِّينِ.”
The section asks what it means to deny the settled account; after recalling human creation, this ayah asks “فَمَا يُكَذِّبُكَ بَعْدُ بِالدِّينِ,” what can make you deny the recompense now.
The section's account day is a day when people answer before its owner; this ayah pictures all people standing before the Lord of the worlds.
The section imagines an open ledger; this ayah introduces the record of the wicked as “كِتَابَ الْفُجَّارِ” in Sijjīn.
This continues the record passage at 83:7 by asking what Sijjīn is, focusing the reader on the place or register of the wicked mentioned there.
This answers 83:8: Sijjīn is “كِتَابٌ مَّرْقُومٌ,” a written record, directly echoing the section's account ledger.
The section shows the denier's social failures; this passage sets out the record of the righteous in ʿIlliyyūn, the contrasting record of those who answer well.
This continues the righteous-record passage begun at 83:18 by asking what ʿIlliyyūn is, directing attention to their register.
This answers 83:19 with “كِتَابٌ مَّرْقُومٌ,” a written record, making explicit the other side of the section's account image.
This completes the register description at 83:18–20: those brought near witness it, showing the record is presented and attested.
The section centers dīn as the day of recompense; this ayah asks what can make anyone know what the Day of Dīn is, introducing its gravity.
This repeats and intensifies the question at 82:17 before the passage describes that day, underscoring the account that the section says is denied.
This completes 82:17–18: on that day no soul can do anything for another, and command belongs to Allah, specifying the finality of the account.
The section imagines the account opened; the person given their book in the right hand says “هَاؤُمُ اقْرَءُوا كِتَابِيَهْ,” inviting others to read it.
This explains the confidence at 69:19: the speaker had expected to meet their account, matching the section's insistence that the ledger comes due.
This continues the right-hand-book scene at 69:19–20, stating the person is in a pleasing life as the outcome of the account.
This completes the outcome begun at 69:21 with a high garden, showing the reward beyond the account the section names.
The section's denier rejects the coming account; this counterpart receives the book in the left hand and wishes it had not been given.
This continues the left-hand-book scene at 69:25 with the regretful wish not to know the account, making denial's consequence visible.
This completes the regret at 69:25–26: the speaker wishes death had ended the matter, the opposite of the section's account continuing to its settlement.
The section's ledger is settled; this ayah says the person given their book in the right hand will face an easy reckoning.
This completes the right-hand-book outcome at 84:7 by specifying that the person is called to an easy account.
This completes that easy reckoning with the person returning joyfully to their family, the favorable outcome of an account answered well.
The section's denier refuses the account; here the person given their book behind their back receives the opposite outcome from 84:7's right-hand recipient.
This continues the behind-the-back book scene at 84:10: the person calls for destruction, expressing the consequence of the account.
This completes the outcome at 84:10–11 with burning fire, the contrary recompense to the easy account in 84:7–9.
The section's account is a debt that must be paid; this ayah warns of the day each soul is returned to Allah and fully paid for what it earned, without injustice.
This ayah describes gathering on a day without doubt and each soul being fully paid for what it earned, matching the section's due-account image.
The section's repayment is an account coming due; this ayah says Allah will recompense every soul for what it earned and is swift in reckoning.
This ayah states that every soul is repaid for what it earned and no one is wronged that day, making the section's debt-and-settlement image explicit.
The section's Day of Dīn closes the account; this ayah says every soul is recompensed for what it earned and none is wronged.
This ayah pictures every soul arriving to argue for itself and being fully repaid for its deeds, a concrete scene of the account the section names.
The section's image makes what is owed come due; this ayah says a human being has only what they strove for, grounding the account in one's acts.
This continues the effort-to-recompense passage at 53:39 by saying the effort will be seen, making the account's contents visible.
This completes 53:39–40: the effort is repaid in full, a direct counterpart to the section's sense of dīn as recompense.
The section describes a ledger and account; this ayah sets up just balances for Resurrection Day and says even a mustard seed's weight will be brought forward.
The section's account makes even small dues matter; this ayah says whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it.
This completes the accounting in 99:7 with the same visibility for an atom's weight of evil, so no small act escapes the reckoning.
The section's due-account has an outcome; this ayah says the one whose scales are heavy will have a pleasing life.
This completes 101:6 by naming the pleasing life as the heavy-scaled person's outcome, showing the result of the measure.
This gives the contrary side of 101:6: the one whose scales are light faces an opposing result, like the denier whose due is refused in the section.
This completes the light-scale outcome at 101:8 by naming the abyss as the person's destination.
The section's ledger leads to judgment; this ayah says those whose scales are heavy are the successful ones.
This gives the other side of 23:102: those whose scales are light have lost themselves, a contrary result in the measured account.
The section's account concerns what is owed and paid; this ayah says Allah does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies a good deed, defining the justice of settlement.
The section's dictionary form identifies the Day of Dīn with judgment and recompense; this ayah says the wicked enter it, “يَصْلَوْنَهَا يَوْمَ الدِّينِ,” describing the day in its punitive context.
This completes the punishment description at 82:15 by saying they will not be absent from it, giving the section's denied account an inescapable horizon.
This is the question answered by 74:43–46: what brought the speakers to Saqar; the following answer names neglected prayer, feeding, and denial of the Day of Dīn, completing a scene of consequences.
This completes the confession at 74:46: they say they persisted until certainty came, showing how the denial described in the section ends at death.
This is the warning completed by the next ayah, 41:7, which identifies the warned group as those withholding zakāh and disbelieving in the Hereafter; this ayah contributes the “woe” over that stance.
The section preserves the dictionary idiom كذب عليكم الحج as meaning Hajj became incumbent; this ayah commands, “أَتِمُّوا الْحَجَّ وَالْعُمْرَةَ لِلَّهِ,” making the obligation's object explicit.
The section labels dīn as obedience; this ayah has the Prophet commanded to worship Allah sincerely in dīn, showing the obedience sense in a command to the speaker.
The section's dictionary form glosses dīn as obedience and submission; this ayah says judgment belongs to Allah and “ذَٰلِكَ الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ,” tying dīn to worshipful obedience.
Where the section shows dues refused to the orphan and poor, this ayah requires leniency toward a debtor in hardship and says remission is better, reversing the withholding posture.
